name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
description: Adversaries abuse command and script interpreters such as PowerShell, Bash, Python, or Windows Command Shell to execute malicious commands and scripts directly on targeted hosts.

name: Phishing
description: Adversaries send targeted phishing messages containing malicious email attachments, hyperlinks, or social engineering lures to gain initial access to victim systems or harvest credentials.

name: Valid Accounts
description: Adversaries obtain and abuse existing valid user credentials, domain accounts, or default service accounts to bypass access controls and establish persistence within the enterprise perimeter.

name: Brute Force
description: Adversaries perform automated credential guessing, password spraying, or dictionary attacks across authentication services like SSH, RDP, FTP, or web logins to discover valid account credentials.

name: Network Service Discovery
description: Adversaries scan network IP ranges and ports using SYN stealth probes or port scanners like Nmap to enumerate active hosts, operating systems, listening daemons, and vulnerable services.

name: Endpoint Denial of Service
description: Adversaries perform resource exhaustion attacks such as TCP SYN floods, Smurf ICMP amplifications, or teardrop malformed packet bursts to degrade or crash target systems and network services.

name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
description: Adversaries scan for and exploit known unpatched vulnerabilities (CVEs) in public-facing internet services such as web servers, VPN gateways, databases, or API microservices.

name: Application Layer Protocol
description: Adversaries blend command and control traffic with normal network operations using legitimate application protocols including HTTP, HTTPS, DNS tunneling, or WebSocket channels.

name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
description: Adversaries exfiltrate sensitive corporate documents, database dumps, and credentials through existing command and control communication channels disguised as benign traffic.

name: Data Encrypted for Impact
description: Adversaries encrypt victim files, databases, and backup volumes with cryptographic algorithms (e.g. AES/RSA) to interrupt operational availability and extort ransom payments.

name: OS Credential Dumping
description: Adversaries dump plaintext credentials, Kerberos tickets, and NTLM password hashes from memory structures like LSASS or security databases like SAM to facilitate privilege escalation.

name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
description: Adversaries circumvent platform elevation controls like Windows UAC or Unix sudoers permissions to elevate unprivileged accounts into root or NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges.

name: User Execution
description: Adversaries rely on specific actions by human victims to execute malicious payloads, such as opening an email attachment, running an unverified installer, or clicking a deceptive popup.

name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
description: Adversaries configure system boot or login autostart mechanisms (such as Windows Registry Run keys, startup folders, cron jobs, or systemd services) to maintain persistence across reboots.

name: Process Injection
description: Adversaries inject malicious code into legitimate processes (such as svchost.exe, explorer.exe, or system daemons) to evade detection from signature-based security software.
